title: NEB Class 11 Physics — Circular Motion — 2024
subject: physics
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Define centripetal acceleration. Derive an expression for it.
questions.solution:
**Centripetal acceleration** is the acceleration of a body in circular motion, directed toward the centre of the circle.

Derivation: a particle moves on radius r with uniform speed v. In time Δt it sweeps angle Δθ. The velocity vector turns through the same angle, so the change Δv ≈ v·Δθ (small angles).

a = Δv/Δt = v(Δθ/Δt) = vω = v(v/r) = **v²/r** (equivalently a = ω²r).
questions.knowledgeNote: Centripetal force F = mv²/r is not a new force — it is the name for whatever net force (tension, friction, gravity) provides the centre-seeking acceleration.
questions.answer: **Definition:** centripetal acceleration is the acceleration of uniform circular motion, directed **radially inward (toward the centre)**, of magnitude a = v²/r = ω²r; it changes the velocity's direction at constant speed. **Derivation:** in time Δt the velocity vector rotates through Δθ = vΔt/r. Placing v and v′ tail-to-tail, the velocity triangle is similar to the radius triangle (both isosceles, same angle Δθ), so |Δv|/v = chord/r ≈ (vΔt)/r for small Δt ⟹ |Δv| = v²Δt/r ⟹ **a = v²/r**, pointing along Δv toward the centre; with v = ωr, a = ω²r. **Deep point:** the two similar isosceles triangles are the whole proof — one in space (radii), one in velocity space (vectors).

questions.question: A car takes a turn of radius 50 m at a speed of 10 m/s. What is its angular velocity and centripetal acceleration?
questions.solution:
Angular velocity ω = v/r = 10/50 = **0.2 rad/s**.

Centripetal acceleration ac = v²/r = 100/50 = **2 m/s²** toward the centre of the turn.
questions.knowledgeNote: ω = v/r and T = 2π/ω link the linear and angular descriptions — convert rpm to rad/s before using them.
questions.answer: **ω = v/r** = 10/50 = **0.2 rad/s**; **a = v²/r** = 100/50 = **2 m/s²** toward the centre. **Deep point:** quote the direction — centripetal acceleration without 'toward the centre' is half an answer.

questions.question: Derive the expression for the angle of banking of a curved road, and find the banking angle for a 100 m radius curve taken at 20 m/s. (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.solution:
On a banked curve (angle θ), the normal reaction N has components N sin θ (horizontal, provides centripetal force) and N cos θ (vertical, balances weight).

N sin θ = mv²/r and N cos θ = mg → dividing gives tan θ = **v²/(rg)**.

tan θ = 400/(100 × 10) = 0.4 → θ = **21.8°**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Banking lets the road itself supply the centripetal force, so vehicles need less friction — that is why expressway curves are tilted.
questions.answer: **Derivation:** for a vehicle on a banked road of angle θ (no friction needed), resolve forces: normal reaction N acts perpendicular to the road surface; weight mg vertically down. **Vertical equilibrium:** N cos θ = mg. **Horizontal (centripetal):** N sin θ = mv²/r. **Divide:** tan θ = v²/(rg) ⟹ **θ = tan⁻¹(v²/rg)**. **Calculation:** tan θ = (20)²/(100 × 10) = 400/1000 = 0.4 ⟹ **θ = tan⁻¹(0.4) ≈ 21.8°**. **Deep point:** the two resolved equations are the derivation — vertical for balance, horizontal for the circle — and their ratio eliminates N, leaving tan θ = v²/rg.

questions.question: A stone is whirled in a vertical circle of radius 1 m. What is the minimum velocity it must have at the top of the circle to complete the loop? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.solution:
At the top, both weight and tension point downward: mv²/r = mg + T. The loop is just completed when the string goes slack, T = 0.

v² = gr → v = √(9.8 × 1) ≈ **3.13 m/s**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Minimum top velocity √(gr); the matching bottom velocity is √(5gr) — the 1:√5 ratio is a standard NEB result.
questions.answer: **Condition at the top:** to just complete the loop, the string's tension (or the track's normal force) is zero at the top and gravity alone supplies the centripetal force: mg = mv²_top/r ⟹ **v_top = √(gr)**. **Substitute:** v_top = √(9.8 × 1) = √9.8 ≈ **3.13 m/s**. **Deep point:** 'minimum' in vertical-circle questions always means 'tension/normal force = 0 at the top' — gravity exactly doing the centripetal job is the boundary between completing the loop and falling away.

questions.question: A conical pendulum has a string 1 m long making 30° with the vertical. Calculate its period of revolution. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.knowledgeNote: The period depends on the vertical height h = l cos θ, not on the mass of the bob.
questions.answer: **Conical pendulum:** the bob moves in a horizontal circle; the string traces a cone. **Resolve:** T cos θ = mg (vertical); T sin θ = mv²/r (horizontal, centripetal), with r = L sin θ. **Period:** T sin θ/T cos θ = v²/(rg) ⟹ tan θ = v²/(rg); with v = 2πr/T_time: **T_time = 2π√(L cos θ/g)**. **Substitute:** L = 1 m, θ = 30°, cos 30° = 0.866: T_time = 2π√(1 × 0.866/9.8) = 2π√0.0884 = 2π × 0.297 ≈ **1.87 s**. **Deep point:** the conical pendulum's period depends on the *horizontal* projection (L cos θ), not the string length — a shorter effective pendulum swings faster, which is why θ ↑ gives a shorter period.

questions.question: A wheel of diameter 0.8 m rotates at 300 revolutions per minute. Find its angular velocity and the linear speed of a point on its rim.
questions.solution:
Frequency f = 300/60 = 5 rev/s.

ω = 2πf = 10π ≈ **31.4 rad/s**.

Rim speed v = ωr = 31.4 × 0.4 ≈ **12.6 m/s**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Always convert rpm → rev/s → rad/s first; most NEB errors here come from using rpm directly in v = ωr.
questions.answer: **Angular velocity:** ω = 2πN/60 = 2π × 300/60 = **31.4 rad/s**. **Radius:** r = d/2 = 0.4 m. **Linear speed:** v = ωr = 31.4 × 0.4 = **12.6 m/s**. **Deep point:** the diameter-to-radius step is the only trap — ω comes from the rotation rate, but v = ωr needs the radius, not the diameter.
